transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-28
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Aisha Coleman (Rivermark Head of Platform), Ben Ortiz (Rivermark ML), Sanjay Rao (Rivermark Infra), Maya Li (Rivermark Product)

Summary:
Weekly POC sync focused on latency tuning: first-token time (TTFT), streaming behavior, sequence length tradeoffs, and kernel selection. Reviewed latest benchmark numbers Redwood ran on dedicated cluster, discussed discrepancy on Rivermark's smoke tests, and agreed on next steps (shared spreadsheets, kernel deep dive, 1k streaming run).

Topics:
- TTFT regressions when enabling streaming on long prefix caching
- p50/p90 changes between 256 and 1024 sequence lengths
- kernel selection mismatches on GCP A2 vs internal prod rigs
- impact of KV cache and prefix warmup

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll keep this to 45 minutes, agenda — quick benchmark review, then kernel and streaming questions, and wrap with next steps. Marco, want to kick off with the numbers?
[00:18] Marco Diaz: yeah, sure. so we re-ran the 512 and 1024 seq profiles on the dedicated pool last night. TTFT for the 512 set was about 110 ms median and 240 ms p90 with streaming off, and with streaming on we saw TTFT go up to ~150 ms p50 and p90 around 310 ms. some of that is serialization overhead and early token flush.
[00:42] Ben Ortiz: wait — that jump looks bigger than we saw. our smoke run on the A2s had p90 around 280 with streaming on. are you using the same kernel flags?
[00:55] Marco Diaz: good question. there might be a mismatch — on our dedicated cluster we used kernel-family v2.3 which defaults to fused-attn kernels, while the A2s we saw earlier were on v2.1 with non-fused. that difference can add 10-30% in tail. also their batch shaping was different — we used continuous batching with target batch size 16, their test was single-request.
[01:20] Aisha Coleman: just to call out constraints — for the POC we need p90 under 350ms for user-facing flows and TTFT under 200 for interactive agents. that's the acceptance bar.
[01:33] Lena Park: got it — those are the SLOs we've been optimizing for. Marco, any quick notes on sequence length tradeoffs?
[01:40] Marco Diaz: yes, the short story is: as you increase seq length, KV cache warms up and per-token throughput improves, but TTFT can worsen for the first token because larger attention kernels pick different execution paths. for 256 seq we saw median TTFT ~95 ms, p90 ~210 ms. for 1024 seq, median token stepping is great but initial TTFT goes to 180-220 ms depending on kernel.
[02:05] Sanjay Rao: are those runs with prefix caching enabled? we noticed when we enabled prefix caching locally the first few requests after a cache eviction were much slower — like 400ms p90.
[02:18] Marco Diaz: yeah, prefix caching helps for steady-state but cold-starts can be worse. we think Rivermark's setup has shorter TTLs on KV cache which explains the spikes.
[02:30] Maya Li: can you explain the streaming interaction? we turned streaming on to improve perceived latency but Ben mentioned TTFT increased, why is that?
[02:40] Marco Diaz: streaming introduces a small buffering window — Redwood's streamer collects a few tokens or partial logits before flushing, so you trade raw TTFT for smoother throughput and reduced tail for long responses. if your front-end expects no buffer, perceived first token might be delayed. also some of it is the framing + JSON marshalling on our side, which we can tune.
[03:05] Ben Ortiz: ok that matches. our test had very small responses (2-4 tokens) so the buffer added relative overhead.
[03:12] Lena Park: actionable item — Marco will produce a config that reduces buffer threshold for short responses and show the tradeoff in cost & tail.
[03:20] Marco Diaz: yep will do. also we recommend trying the micro-batching mode at the infra level; that tends to reduce p90 without hurting TTFT when your request mix has many tiny responses.
[03:33] Aisha Coleman: question on kernel choice — you said fused-attn gave better steady throughput. does that mean we have to switch kernels on our GCP A2s? what about quantization impact?
[03:45] Marco Diaz: fused-attn is generally faster on Ampere+ families with good memory layout. on older kernels or certain drivers, the fallback path can be slower. quantization helps memory and throughput but can increase CPU-side dequant overhead that impacts TTFT slightly. we recommend model-quantize Q4_0 for throughput experiments and measure TTFT impact.
[04:10] Sanjay Rao: our infra team is sensitive to kernel changes. can you provide exact kernel flags and a validated list of driver versions?
[04:18] Marco Diaz: yes, I'll share a kernel-selection table: flags, driver version, expected p50/p90 deltas. that'll be in the benchmark sheet.
[04:25] Ben Ortiz: on the subject of streaming vs non-streaming, one more datapoint: when we enabled streaming with 256 seq on A2, p90 dropped for long responses but TTFT rose by ~30ms. is there a recommended hybrid approach?
[04:40] Marco Diaz: hybrid is what we use: dynamic streaming — if expected response length < 8 tokens, disable streaming and use single-shot fast path; otherwise enable streaming. that logic can live in the SDK or at the router level.
[04:52] Maya Li: is that something Redwood can expose as a config in the SDK? we'd prefer not to build routing logic ourselves.
[04:58] Lena Park: yes, we've got a config toggle and we'll add a suggested policy sample that you can drop in.
[05:06] Aisha Coleman: okay good, timeline question — we need to sign off on latency behavior by EoQ (end of quarter). what's realistic?
[05:12] Marco Diaz: with the kernel tuning and dynamic streaming policy plus micro-batching, we think p90 under 350ms is realistic for your observed mix. it will require the 1k run and one kernel pass to validate.
[05:24] Sanjay Rao: one more technical detail — KV cache TTLs, what do you recommend for our use case? we have many short-lived sessions.
[05:32] Marco Diaz: lower TTLs reduce stale cache size but increase cold cache events. you can use a two-tier approach: short TTL for session-specific prefixes, longer TTL for common system prompts. also warm-prefix endpoints on deployment change helps.
[05:48] Ben Ortiz: can you also share what you mean by 'warm-prefix endpoint'? we've seen docs but not a sample flow.
[05:54] Marco Diaz: it's basically an internal priming request that populates the KV cache for a model variant before traffic hits it, we have a script we'll share.
[06:02] Lena Park: ok, let's go over the benchmark numbers quickly — Marco, pull the sheet?
[06:06] Marco Diaz: yes. so summary numbers (last night's run): 256 seq non-streaming p50 TTFT 95ms p90 210ms; 512 non-streaming p50 110ms p90 240ms; 512 streaming p50 150ms p90 310ms; 1024 non-streaming p50 130ms p90 290ms. cost per 1M tokens estimated in sheet, I'll attach.
[06:32] Aisha Coleman: our runs showed a slightly higher TTFT at 512 — I suspect different driver and single-request testing. we'll upload logs to the shared folder by tomorrow.
[06:40] Lena Park: perfect — that aligns with next steps. Recap\/Next steps: Marco to share kernel table and lowered streamer config; Lena to send benchmark sheet and cost calc; Ben to run 1k streaming-enabled run and upload logs.
[06:55] Marco Diaz: I'll also add a small patch you can run that toggles buffer threshold and micro-batching flags.
[07:02] Sanjay Rao: can we follow up with a kernel deep dive next Tue? our infra and hardware folks want to join.
[07:08] Lena Park: scheduled — I'll send a calendar invite for Tue 10am PT.
[07:12] Maya Li: thanks all, that was helpful.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker labels are mostly correct though a few words (kernels, KV cache) may be transcribed as "kernel-family v2.3" vs internal naming; some filler words and ums remain.
